Seed the queue with several sources at once instead of one, and the result is, for every vertex, the distance to the nearest of them — one pass, not one pass per source. A grid with three spreading fires answers 'when does the fire reach this cell' in a single multi-source sweep.

Edges weighted only 0 or 1 need no priority queue at all: push a 0-weight edge's endpoint to the front of a deque, a 1-weight edge's endpoint to the back. The deque's own order stays non-decreasing in distance, and the answer matches Dijkstra's algorithm on the identical graph.
Two-colour a five-cycle, alternating colour outward from one vertex — can it finish without ever giving two neighbours the same colour?

BFS 2-colours a graph by alternating colour at each frontier step; it is bipartite exactly when this never assigns the same colour to both endpoints of an edge. The first edge where it does, together with the BFS-tree paths back to their common ancestor, is itself an odd cycle — a witness, not just a verdict.

at.step: On a low-diameter, high-degree graph — a social network, not a road network — the frontier can become most of the graph in a single step, and scanning its own many outgoing edges gets expensive fast. Direction-optimizing BFS switches: once the frontier is large, unvisited vertices scan for a frontier neighbour instead, examining far fewer edges for the same step.

at.step: A breadth-first frontier answers one question well: the fewest edges to reach a vertex. It says nothing about which vertex to visit next when the graph has structure a single widening ring can't see — a dependency that must come before another, a group of vertices that can all reach each other and nothing outside the group. Those answers come from visiting as deep as possible before backtracking, not level by level.

items.item: BFS's shortest-path guarantee follows purely from the FIFO queue's own ordering: a vertex at distance d is enqueued only after every vertex at distance d-1 has already been dequeued, so no shorter path can arrive later

at.step: A FIFO queue holds the current frontier: dequeue a vertex, enqueue every neighbour not yet seen. Every vertex at distance d is dequeued before any vertex at distance d+1 is ever enqueued, so the first time a vertex is reached, its distance is already final — the proof the chapter's opening question asked for.

items.item: Multi-source BFS is not k separate searches merged afterward — seeding the queue with every source at distance zero simultaneously gives, for every vertex, the distance to its nearest source in one pass costing O(n+m), not O(k(n+m))

at.step: Seed the queue with several sources at once instead of one, and the result is, for every vertex, the distance to the nearest of them — one pass, not one pass per source. A grid with three spreading fires answers 'when does the fire reach this cell' in a single multi-source sweep.

items.item: 0-1 BFS's deque ordering is a special case of the general principle behind Dijkstra's priority queue: it keeps the frontier processed in non-decreasing distance order, but a deque suffices only because every edge weight is 0 or 1, never a general non-negative weight

at.step: Edges weighted only 0 or 1 need no priority queue at all: push a 0-weight edge's endpoint to the front of a deque, a 1-weight edge's endpoint to the back. The deque's own order stays non-decreasing in distance, and the answer matches Dijkstra's algorithm on the identical graph.

items.item: The bipartiteness-by-2-colouring test works with either BFS or DFS as the underlying traversal; BFS's version alternates colour by frontier layer, which is why the witness uses BFS-tree paths rather than DFS discovery order

at.step: BFS 2-colours a graph by alternating colour at each frontier step; it is bipartite exactly when this never assigns the same colour to both endpoints of an edge. The first edge where it does, together with the BFS-tree paths back to their common ancestor, is itself an odd cycle — a witness, not just a verdict.

items.item: Direction-optimizing BFS changes only which vertices scan which edges each round, never the algorithm's own answer (still the same unweighted shortest distances) — the speedup is purely in edges examined, not a different result

at.step: On a low-diameter, high-degree graph — a social network, not a road network — the frontier can become most of the graph in a single step, and scanning its own many outgoing edges gets expensive fast. Direction-optimizing BFS switches: once the frontier is large, unvisited vertices scan for a frontier neighbour instead, examining far fewer edges for the same step.

items.item: The same FIFO-frontier idea underlies every variant in this topic: multi-source BFS only changes the queue's seeding, 0-1 BFS only changes which end of the container an edge's endpoint is pushed to, and bipartiteness only adds a colour label — none of them are new algorithms

at.step: A graph with a billion edges can still answer 'how many people separate you from this stranger' in a handful of steps, because the people worth checking next are never more than one step past the people already checked — a widening ring, never a wrong turn.

items.item: An undirected graph's BFS tree has no forward or cross edges in the DFS sense, since every edge either joins two vertices in the same or adjacent layers — a fact topic 60's edge classification will state in full for DFS, used here only informally to justify the 2-colouring witness construction

The first edge where it does, together with the BFS-tree paths back to their common ancestor, is itself an odd cycle — a witness, not just a verdict.

items.item: Direction-optimizing BFS's bottom-up step needs the inverse graph when the input is directed, since 'does any neighbour of mine belong to the frontier' is itself a query over incoming edges, not outgoing ones

0-1 BFS generalises to k-weight BFS with k+1 buckets (a bucket queue) rather than a plain deque, the structural reason the deque trick is specific to the 0/1 case and not a general substitute for Dijkstra's heap
